entities.summary: The Monad is sovereign, with nothing above it. It is God and Parent, the Father of the All. It is the Invisible Spirit, the pure light upon which no eye can gaze. It is not among the things that exist, but is far greater. It is the head of all realms and sustains them through its goodness. It is eternal because it needs nothing, for it is absolutely complete.
entities.overview: In the Sethian cosmological framework represented here, the Monad stands beyond the ordered divine realms and beyond every lower cosmological structure. The Apocryphon of John describes the supreme source through apophatic language: invisible, immeasurable, incorruptible, ineffable and beyond comprehension. Rather than existing as one being among others, it is the ultimate transcendent source from which the higher divine order unfolds.

sourceTerms: God and Father of the All
terminology.note: The major English translations preserve different opening renderings. Frederik Wisse uses The Monad; Marvin Meyer uses The One; Karen L. King renders the shorter recension as The Unity and the longer recension as The Monad. The Invisible Spirit and related designations recur throughout the source. These Sethian terms remain separate from Bythos, which belongs to the Valentinian comparative layer.

primaryLens.interpretiveFrame: The supreme principle is radically transcendent, preceding the Pleroma and every spatial, temporal, material and aeonic structure.

researchNotes.ontologicalPriority: The Monad is represented outside the Pleroma in the visualization because it functions as the transcendent source prior to the ordered divine Fullness.
researchNotes.apophaticCharacter: The source relies heavily on negative or apophatic description: the supreme principle exceeds ordinary predicates, measurement, form and comprehension.
researchNotes.terminologyCaution: The Frederik Wisse translation explicitly begins this discourse with “The Monad is a monarchy with nothing above it,” while Invisible Spirit is the recurrent designation throughout the passage. The title is therefore source-grounded in this translation but not treated as terminology exclusive to Sethianism.
researchNotes.bythosCaution: Bythos is a Valentinian term for the primal Depth and is not displayed as a direct Sethian alternative name for the Monad.
researchNotes.crossSourceCaution: The Gospel of the Egyptians provides closely related Sethian language concerning the Great Invisible Spirit, but terminology from that text should remain source-attributed when it is not independently explicit in the Apocryphon of John.
researchNotes.allogenesParallel: Allogenes the Stranger, NHC XI,3 62–64, provides a distinct Sethian parallel for apophatic description of the transcendent principle. It is displayed as a parallel source, not as another witness to the wording of the Apocryphon of John.

comparativeTraditions.name: Bythos — The Depth in Valentinian Pleromatic Theology
comparativeTraditions.description: In the Valentinian system, Bythos, the primordial Depth, stands at the beginning of the Pleromatic genealogy and is paired with Ennoea or Sige. Bythos offers a comparison with the transcendent Sethian source, but it belongs to a distinct Valentinian structure and is not presented as a direct alternative name used by The Apocryphon of John.

sourceAttestations.role: ancient heresiological witness to Bythos at the beginning of the Valentinian Pleromatic genealogy

comparativeTraditions.name: The Platonic / Middle-Platonic One
comparativeTraditions.description: Middle-Platonic and later Platonic traditions describe a transcendent first principle above ordinary predicates; in later Platonism, differentiated levels of reality proceed from the One. This provides an important philosophical comparison with the Sethian Invisible Spirit, while the two should not be treated as identical concepts.
sourceCitations: JOHN D. TURNER, SETHIAN GNOSTICISM AND THE PLATONIC TRADITION

entities.summary: Barbelo is the first Thought and first power to come forth from the Invisible Spirit, the Spirit’s perfect image and the Forethought of the All. The source names her the Mother-Father, the Womb of Everything, the First Human and the Holy Spirit. At her request, Foreknowledge, Incorruptibility, Eternal Life and Truth come forth and stand with her, forming the first aeonic complex.
entities.overview: In the Apocryphon of John, Barbelo emerges in immediate relation to the supreme Invisible Spirit. She is presented as the first Thought or Forethought, the image of the Invisible Spirit, the first power and the first to come forth. Barbelo occupies a pivotal position between the radically transcendent source and the further articulation of the divine realm.

primaryLens.interpretiveFrame: Barbelo represents the first articulated divine reality in relation to the transcendent Invisible Spirit and becomes the locus through which the higher divine realm begins to unfold.

researchNotes.textualTransmission: The description and titulary of Barbelo should be checked across the four surviving Coptic witnesses.
researchNotes.relationshipCaution: The relationship between the Invisible Spirit and Barbelo should be represented according to the language of the source.

entities.notes: Barbelo is retained as a distinct primary entity because the Apocryphon of John gives this figure a central structural role in the unfolding of the transcendent divine realm.

pleromaticProcess.explorerTitle: Explore Barbelo and the Four Aeons
pleromaticProcess.introduction: Barbelo is herself counted as the first aeon in this divine complex. At her request, Foreknowledge, Incorruptibility, Eternal Life and Truth come forth from the Invisible Spirit and stand with her. Barbelo together with these four powers forms the five aeons of the Father.

entries.name: Foreknowledge
entries.description: At Barbelo’s request, Foreknowledge comes forth from the Invisible Spirit and stands with her. Foreknowledge is a distinct aeonic power and must not be confused with Forethought, which designates Barbelo herself.

entries.name: Incorruptibility
entries.description: Incorruptibility comes forth at Barbelo’s request and stands with her within the first aeonic complex.

entries.name: Eternal Life
entries.description: Eternal Life comes forth at Barbelo’s request and joins the divine powers gathered around her.

entries.name: Truth
entries.description: Truth is the fourth power requested by Barbelo and completes the group that stands with her.

note.name: The Five Aeons and the Ten Aeons
note.description: The text calls Barbelo and these four powers the five aeons of the Father. Because the five are described as androgynous, they are also counted as ten. The five aeons and the ten aeons therefore describe the same divine complex, not two successive groups.

primarySourceCitations: THE SECRET BOOK OF JOHN (THE APOCRYPHON OF JOHN), NHC II,1; III,1; IV,1; BG 8502,2
parallelSourceCitations: THREE FORMS OF FIRST THOUGHT (TRIMORPHIC PROTENNOIA), NHC XIII,1

entities.summary: When the Father gazes upon Barbelo through the pure light surrounding the Invisible Spirit, she conceives and brings forth a spark of light, radiant like the blessed light, though not as great. This pure light is the only Child of the Mother-Father, her sole offspring. The Invisible Spirit rejoices in the Child, anoints him with his own goodness until he becomes perfect, lacking nothing, and establishes him over all things. Thus the divine Autogenes comes forth as the Anointed, the Christ. From Autogenes, through the gift of the Spirit, the Four Great Luminaries come forth, opening the next unfolding of the Pleroma.
entities.overview: Anointed with the goodness of the Invisible Spirit and established over all things, Autogenes becomes the divine source from whom the Four Great Luminaries come forth.

primaryLens.interpretiveFrame: Autogenes functions as a major divine figure within the higher aeonic order.

researchNotes.conceptualCaution: The title Christ in this context should not automatically be collapsed into later orthodox Christological categories.

entities.notes: Autogenes is included in the primary view because it marks a major structural transition within the higher divine order.

entries.name: Mind
entries.subtitle: The Fellow Worker
entries.description: Autogenes asks that Mind be given to him as a fellow worker, and the Invisible Spirit grants the request.

entries.name: Will
entries.subtitle: Intention Becoming Act
entries.description: Will emerges as divine intention takes effective form, joining Mind in the articulation of creative activity.

entries.name: Word
entries.subtitle: Divine Activity Expressed
entries.description: Word follows Will and becomes the expressive means through which Autogenes brings the spiritual order into articulation.

entries.name: The Attending Divine Powers
entries.description: Eternal Life, Will, Mind, and Foreknowledge attend Autogenes and glorify the Invisible Spirit and Barbelo.

note.name: A Preparatory Sequence
note.description: This sequence describes the articulation of divine activity around Autogenes. It should not be treated as a second list of the Twelve Aeons or confused with the Four Great Luminaries that emerge next.

primarySourceCitations: THE SECRET BOOK OF JOHN (THE APOCRYPHON OF JOHN), NHC II,1; III,1; IV,1; BG 8502,2
parallelSourceCitations: THE GOSPEL OF JUDAS, CODEX TCHACOS

comparativeTraditions.name: Ptah and the Memphite Cosmogony
comparativeTraditions.description: In the Memphite Theology preserved on the Shabaka Stone, creation proceeds through Ptah’s heart and tongue: what is conceived in the heart is brought forth through speech. This offers a bounded comparison with the divine Self-Generated creating through the Word, without identifying Ptah with Autogenes or the Invisible Spirit.
sourceCitations: THE MEMPHITE THEOLOGY (SHABAKA STONE), BM EA 498

sourceAttestations.role: primary Egyptian evidence for creation articulated through heart and tongue

comparativeTraditions.name: Creation Through Divine Speech in Genesis
comparativeTraditions.description: Genesis presents creation unfolding through divine speech: God speaks, and what is spoken comes to be. The comparison concerns the creative power of the spoken word; the biblical creator and the Sethian Autogenes remain distinct.

sourceAttestations.role: scriptural intertext for creation unfolding through divine speech

comparativeTraditions.name: The Word in John 1
comparativeTraditions.description: John 1 places the Word in the beginning and declares that all things came into being through it. This forms a close textual comparison with Autogenes creating through the Word, while the Johannine Word and the Sethian Self-Generated are not presented as the same figure.

sourceAttestations.role: scriptural Logos intertext for all things coming into being through the Word

entities.summary: The first of the Four Great Luminaries, emanated from the divine Autogenes. Armozel presides over the first aeonic triad within the ordered structure of the Pleroma: Grace (Charis), Truth (Aletheia), and Form (Morphē).
entities.notes: Armozel appears through the Four Luminaries group.
entities.overview:
The first of the Four Great Luminaries, established within the aeonic order of Autogenes. The perfect archetypal human, Geradamas (Pigera-Adamas), is placed in this first realm beside Armozel and the great Autogenes Christ.

Presiding over the first aeonic triad: Grace (Charis), Truth (Aletheia), and Form (Morphē).

aeonicPosition.sequenceMeaning: First luminary and first aeonic domain in the fourfold structure.

researchNotes.function: Armozel structures the first of the four luminary domains and is associated with Grace, Truth and Form.
researchNotes.crossTextStatus: The four-luminary pattern is attested in multiple Sethian texts, but functions, associated figures and terminology can vary by source.
researchNotes.pairingCaution: Related Sethian texts may describe consorts of the luminaries. Such cross-text evidence should be identified by source and not silently imported into the Apocryphon of John reconstruction.

sourceAttestations.role: second luminary

entities.summary: The second of the Four Great Luminaries, emanated from the divine Autogenes. Oroiael presides over the second aeonic triad within the ordered structure of the Pleroma: Afterthought (Epinoia), Perception (Aisthēsis), and Memory (Mnēmē).
entities.notes: Oroiael appears through the Four Luminaries group.
entities.overview:
The second great aeon of light. It governs the realm of intellect, mental perception, and conceptualization. This sphere of light is the spiritual dwelling place of Seth, the spiritual son of the archetypal human Geradamas (Adamas), ancestor of the Gnostic spiritual race and archetype of the enlightened soul.

Presiding over the second aeonic triad: Afterthought (Epinoia), Perception (Aisthēsis), and Memory (Mnēmē).

researchNotes.interpretiveCaution: The description of Oroiael as governing intellect, mental perception and conceptualization is an explanatory interpretation of the aeonic structure rather than a literal functional title stated by the Apocryphon of John.

entities.summary: The third of the Four Great Luminaries, emanated from the divine Autogenes. Daveithai presides over the third aeonic triad within the ordered structure of the Pleroma: Understanding (Synesis), Love (Agapē), and Idea (Idea).
entities.notes: Daveithai appears through the Four Luminaries group.
entities.overview:
The third great aeon of light. It governs the emotional and relational dimensions of the divine realm, specifically divine love and deep understanding. It houses the seed of Seth, the lineage of enlightened Gnostic souls who descend into the material world but ultimately belong to the Pleroma.

Presiding over the third aeonic triad: Understanding (Synesis), Love (Agapē), and Idea.

entities.summary: The fourth of the Four Great Luminaries, emanated from the divine Autogenes. Eleleth presides over the fourth and final aeonic triad within the ordered structure of the Pleroma: Perfection (Teleiotēs), Peace (Eirēnē), and Sophia (Wisdom).
entities.notes: Eleleth appears through the Four Luminaries group.
entities.overview:
The fourth of the Four Great Luminaries, established over the fourth divine realm. In this realm are placed the souls of those who were initially ignorant of the Fullness and did not repent immediately, but later turned back. Sophia occupies the third position in Eleleth's triad, immediately before the narrative turns to her independent act of generation.

Presiding over the fourth aeonic triad: Perfection (Teleiotēs), Peace (Eirēnē), and Sophia (Wisdom).

sourceAttestations.notes: Sophia brings forth an offspring without the agreement of her consort. The offspring becomes Yaldabaoth.

entities.summary: The 3rd aeon in Eleleth's triad and 12/12 in this editorial sequence. Sophia then becomes an active figure: her independent generation without the participation of her consort leads toward Yaldabaoth and the lower cosmological order.
entities.overview: Sophia, or Wisdom, is the third member of Eleleth's triad after Perfection and Peace. In the editorial sequence used by Anamnesis Mundi, this places Sophia at position 12 of 12. Unlike most members of the twelve-aeon listing, Sophia immediately becomes an active figure in the narrative. She seeks to bring forth a likeness from herself without the participation of her consort and without the approval of the Spirit. The resulting generation becomes the decisive transition toward Yaldabaoth and the lower cosmological order.

primaryLens.interpretiveFrame: Sophia stands at the threshold between the ordered higher divine realm and the emergence of the deficient lower order.

researchNotes.structuralImportance: Sophia forms the principal narrative bridge between the higher aeonic order and the appearance of Yaldabaoth.
researchNotes.interpretiveCaution: The episode should not be reduced to a simple moralized concept of a fall.
researchNotes.materialContinuity: Sophia's relationship to the power carried by Yaldabaoth and to the later material and human orders must be reconstructed separately from the textual evidence.
researchNotes.aeonicPosition: Sophia is the third member of Eleleth's triad, after Perfection and Peace, and is displayed as 12/12 in the editorial sequence reconstructed from the source order.
researchNotes.consortCaution: The Apocryphon of John makes the absence of Sophia's consort or partner explicit in the generation episode. A specific name for that consort should not be supplied unless supported by a cited source.
researchNotes.crossTraditionCaution: Valentinian and other Gnostic systems organize aeons and syzygies differently. Their pairings must not be imported into this Sethian reconstruction without explicit labeling.
researchNotes.functionStatus: The source explicitly places this aeon within a luminary triad. A separate individual action or office should not be inferred unless the text states one.

entities.notes: Sophia is retained as a primary timeline node because her episode changes the direction of the cosmological narrative.

consortContext.apocryphonOfJohn: The narrative explicitly states that Sophia acts without the agreement or participation of her consort/partner, but this database does not assign a name to that consort unless a specific textual witness supports it.
consortContext.structuralMeaning: The absence of the consort is narratively significant because Sophia's generation occurs outside the ordered mode of divine generation described by the source.

sourceAttestations.role: chief ruler of the lower order
sourceAttestations.notes: Yaldabaoth is generated by Sophia, receives great power from his Mother, separates himself from his place of origin, establishes another aeon and generates subordinate authorities.

sourceAttestations.role: carrier of power originating from Sophia
sourceAttestations.notes: The source distinguishes Yaldabaoth's own fire from the power of light received from his Mother. This maternal power remains important later in the anthropogonic narrative.

entities.summary: The chief ruler of the lower demiurgic order, who generates and commands the archons through whom the lower cosmos is fashioned and humanity is formed.
entities.overview: In the Apocryphon of John, Yaldabaoth emerges from Sophia's independent generation and is placed outside the higher immortal realm. He receives great power from his Mother but does not understand the transcendent source from which that power ultimately derives. He establishes a separate aeonic domain and generates subordinate rulers and authorities. The text therefore presents Yaldabaoth as both dependent upon a power originating above him and ignorant of that origin. His subsequent activity becomes central to the organization of the lower cosmos and to the formation of humanity.

terminology.note: Names and spellings vary among manuscript witnesses and modern translations. Saklas and Samael function as additional names or designations of the Chief Ruler in the source tradition.

inheritedPower.description: Yaldabaoth possesses a power whose origin is traced to Sophia. This continuity is not presented as a voluntary transfer from Sophia to Yaldabaoth.
inheritedPower.distinguishedFrom: The source distinguishes this maternal light-power from the fire that Yaldabaoth distributes among subordinate rulers.
inheritedPower.laterTrajectory: The maternal power becomes important again in the formation and animation of the human being.

primaryLens.interpretiveFrame: Yaldabaoth is an ignorant lower ruler who possesses power derived from Sophia while remaining unaware of the higher divine reality from which that power ultimately originates.

researchNotes.powerContinuity: The text explicitly establishes continuity between Sophia and the power possessed by Yaldabaoth. This continuity must be tracked through later stages of the narrative.
researchNotes.fireVsLight: The source differentiates the ruler's distributed fire from the higher light-power received from Sophia. These categories should not be collapsed.
researchNotes.materialFormation: The exact relationship among Yaldabaoth, the subordinate rulers, elemental matter and the later construction of the material cosmos requires a dedicated event-level reconstruction.
researchNotes.humanContinuity: In the anthropogonic episode, the power originating from the Mother is transferred from Yaldabaoth into the human form. This will require an explicit relationship chain in the database.
researchNotes.interpretiveCaution: Yaldabaoth should not be presented simply as the absolute creator of substance ex nihilo. The source depicts him as operating with powers and models whose origins precede him.
researchNotes.agencyCaution: Language implying that Sophia voluntarily gave matter, light or creative power to Yaldabaoth should be avoided unless explicitly required by a particular source. The narrative sequence should distinguish unintended consequence from deliberate transmission.
researchNotes.comparativeCaution: Possible identifications or comparisons with deities, biblical figures or creator concepts from other traditions should remain in the comparative layer unless directly supported by the historical evidence.

comparativeTraditions.name: The Platonic Demiurge
comparativeTraditions.description: Yaldabaoth can be compared with the Demiurge of Plato's Timaeus because both occupy a formative role in relation to the cosmos. The resemblance is accompanied by a fundamental reversal: Plato's Demiurge orders the cosmos by reference to an intelligible model, whereas Yaldabaoth acts in ignorance of the higher divine reality.
sourceCitations: JOHN D. TURNER, SETHIAN GNOSTICISM AND THE PLATONIC TRADITION

sourceAttestations.role: primary Platonic evidence for the good craftsman ordering the cosmos according to an intelligible model
scholarly context for the bounded comparison between Sethian myth and Platonic tradition
sourceAttestations.notes: Supports comparison without identifying Yaldabaoth with Plato’s Demiurge.

comparativeTraditions.name: The Biblical Creator
comparativeTraditions.description: Yaldabaoth's declarations of exclusive divinity echo biblical language asserting that there is no other God. In the Sethian narrative this language is radically recontextualized: the claim exposes Yaldabaoth's ignorance because a transcendent divine reality exists above him.
sourceCitations: THE SECRET BOOK OF JOHN (THE APOCRYPHON OF JOHN), NHC II,1; III,1; IV,1; BG 8502,2

sourceAttestations.role: biblical source for declarations that there is no other God
primary Sethian evidence for the recontextualized declaration placed in Yaldabaoth’s mouth

comparativeTraditions.name: The Seth-Typhon Tradition
comparativeTraditions.description: Some scholarship has explored Greco-Egyptian traditions surrounding Seth-Typhon as part of the cultural background against which an arrogant or negatively characterized lower ruler could be imagined. This does not identify Yaldabaoth with Seth or Typhon; it indicates a possible mythic-historical environment in which related motifs could be reworked.
sourceCitations: TUOMAS RASIMUS, PARADISE RECONSIDERED IN GNOSTIC MYTHMAKING, CH. 3

sourceAttestations.role: modern scholarly analysis of Seth-Typhon, Ophite and Sethian creator traditions
sourceAttestations.notes: Supports a possible mythic-historical context, not an identity between Yaldabaoth and Seth-Typhon.

entities.notes: Yaldabaoth marks the beginning of the Demiurgic Order phase. The formation of the archons, the lower heavens, elemental matter and the material cosmos will be represented separately rather than compressed into this entry.

subordinateStructure.laterDistributionStatement: After naming the twelve authorities, the long recension states that Yaldabaoth set up seven kings over the seven heavens and five over the depth of the abyss.
subordinateStructure.mappingStatus: The naming passage does not explicitly map the first seven and last five names of the twelve-authority list to those later seven-and-five offices. Anamnesis Mundi therefore keeps the statements separate.
subordinateStructure.recensionCaution: The short recension preserves a different naming and organizational pattern and should be modeled separately.

primarySourceCitations: THE SECRET BOOK OF JOHN (THE APOCRYPHON OF JOHN), NHC II,1; III,1; IV,1; BG 8502,2
entities.contextualNote: Only after the creation had gathered around him and the multitude of angels who had come forth from him stood at his side did Yaldabaoth speak: “I am a jealous god and there is no other god beside me.” But his words reveal more than he intends: the text says that by claiming this, he lets his angels know that another God exists, for without another, there would be no one to envy (NHC II,1 13,8–9).
